clue.text: Total eclipse enthralling smart guy

indicators.note: To enthral is to hold somebody captive, and these two words are holding four consecutive letters captive between them.

parts.note: four letters in a row here, starting partway through the first word and crossing the gap

explanation.surface: A complete blackout of the sun holding some clever man spellbound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enthralling' does nothing to the letters except hold them still, which is the quietest kind of instruction. Alec is the crossword's clever one, from the phrase smart Alec.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart Alec is a know-all, and the name carries that sense on its own, so 'smart guy' points straight at the man in the phrase.

clue.text: Star's name shortened, in slang

indicators.note: Shortening a word takes something off its end, so the name arrives one letter lighter than it was given.

parts.note: the north star is named for the pole it stands over

explanation.surface: A famous star's name, clipped the way street talk clips things.
explanation.walkthrough: Polari was the coded slang of gay Britain and the theatre, kept alive on radio by Julian and Sandy in Round the Horne. The setter needs only one letter off a star.
explanation.definitionFit: Polari is one particular slang — the coded vocabulary of gay and theatrical Britain — so the definition names it by its category rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Feasting king has a small herbal brew, interrupted by short nap?

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are broken into by the nap letters, which go inside them
a brew is something mixed and stewed, so these letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: zzz stands for sleep in cartoons, and a short one loses a Z

explanation.surface: A king at a banquet sips a little herbal tea, then dozes off briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brew' looks like the tea, but it is the anagram signal for A, S and HERBAL, giving BELSHAAR, which ZZ splits. Belshazzar's feast, in the Book of Daniel, saw the writing on the wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Belshazzar was the Babylonian king whose great feast is described in the Book of Daniel.

clue.text: Like the usual answer (part)

parts.note: A is the standard short form of answer, the one that sits opposite Q
to part two things is to sever them, cutting one clean from the other

explanation.surface: The same old reply, with a bit of it put in brackets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' is a verb here, not a portion — the parting of two things, which is severing. The brackets look like a note about the enumeration and hold half the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: As ever means as always, so 'like the usual' says the same thing as a comparison and slots into a sentence in the same place.

clue.text: For one, David succeeded opening a handy reader

indicators.note: Opening a thing means cutting a gap into it, and the single letter named before it is what slips into the gap.

parts.note: someone who reads hands for a living is reading palms
s. is the genealogist's mark for succeeded, as in a king who s. his father

explanation.surface: David managed to get a convenient little book open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A handy reader' is a fortune teller rather than a paperback, the hand being the thing she reads. 'For one' is the setter admitting David is an example, not the whole class.
explanation.definitionFit: David is credited with the Psalms, so he is one psalmist among several — the definition works by example, which 'for one' declares.

clue.text: Opportunity coming round to change colour, artist has no hesitation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a chance that comes in rotation, as in 'your turn'
second meaning: a rotation, as in a turn of the wheel
third meaning: as leaves turn in autumn

indicators.note: the artist goes without the hesitation, so those letters are removed

parts.note: J M W Turner was the English landscape painter
er is the sound of hesitating

explanation.surface: A painter gets a chance to switch palettes without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue packs in three definitions before the wordplay: 'has no' removes ER, the hesitation sound, from TURNER, the English landscape painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Turn covers a chance in sequence, a rotation, and a shift of hue, as milk or leaves turn.

clue.text: Round hospital, murderer noticed massacre weapon that was filmed

indicators.note: Going round something means wrapping about it, so the letter for the building ends up enclosed by the name beside it.

parts.note: the Bible's first killer, who murdered his brother Abel
H is hospital on road signs and in the radio alphabet
noticed in the past tense is saw

explanation.surface: On a hospital round somebody notices a murderer holding the weapon from a horror film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' wants to be the doctor's round of the wards and is the wrapping instruction instead. The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is the film the definition has in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre put this tool on screen as a murder weapon, so the definition names it by the film that made it notorious.

clue.text: Penalty would be fit, if this swimmer knocked out

indicators.note: states what the remainder becomes once the swimmer is gone: the word that follows
the swimmer's letters are knocked out of the penalty word, and what remains spells the word fit

parts.note: a forfeit is a penalty paid for a fault

explanation.surface: A conditional rule says a penalty would be justified if a fish were knocked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked out' takes the fish out of FORFEIT, and what is left, F and IT, 'would be' FIT; the clue states the result rather than the starting point.
explanation.definitionFit: The orfe is a freshwater fish of the carp family, often kept in ornamental ponds.

clue.text: Football team 1-1 after leading at first, idiots missing header

definitions.note: The answer is a plural nickname and the definition is a singular collective — a team is one thing made of eleven, and British usage happily treats it as both.

indicators.note: Taken at first means only the very front of the word is wanted, which is one letter of it.
A header is the top or front of a thing, so the word turns up here without its opening letter.
What comes after something is written down behind it, so these two numbers follow the letter already found.

parts.note: the leading letter of that word, taken from the word itself
the first of the pair as a Roman numeral
the second of the pair written out as a word
idiots are asses, and the word arrives without the A at its front

explanation.surface: A side draws 1-1 after going ahead early, and some fools miss a header.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lionesses are England's women's football team. Every word of the surface stays inside one match report — the score, the lead, the missed header — while the wordplay quietly counts letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Lionesses is the nickname of England's women's football team, so the definition names them by exactly what they are.

clue.text: Old teacher's pronouns

parts.note: the first of two, the object form of we
the second, the object form of she, laid straight after the first

explanation.surface: A retired schoolmaster listing the pronouns he goes by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pronouns' reads as the modern habit of stating which ones you use, and it is two of them written end to end. An usher was the assistant master in an old grammar school.
explanation.definitionFit: Usher is the archaic word for an under-master or assistant schoolteacher, a sense now kept alive mainly by crosswords.

clue.text: Charlie brings in bowl for dog's dinner

indicators.note: Bringing a thing in carries it inside what is already there, so the round object ends up within the name.

parts.note: Chas is the familiar short form of Charles
a bowl is a round vessel, and O is the round letter

explanation.surface: Charlie carries a bowl in and the dog gets its dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like the radio alphabet's C and is a man's nickname instead. A dog's dinner is British for a mess: make a dog's dinner of a job and you have botched it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's dinner is British idiom for a shambles, and chaos is that state at full strength — the noun, not the adjective.

clue.text: Card for One Gentleman of Verona

definitions.meaning: the one that goes anonymously through the letterbox on 14 February
Shakespeare's play has two of them, and this is the name of just one

explanation.surface: Somebody posting a card to one of the two gentlemen in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The Two Gentlemen of Verona are Valentine and Proteus, so 'One' is doing arithmetic on a title. The capital G is the play's, and no letters change hands anywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A valentine is the card sent on 14 February, and Valentine is the name of one of the two Veronese gentlemen in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Feature of High Peak in which to disappear

definitions.meaning: go up far enough and there is measurably less of the stuff to breathe
the idiom for vanishing without trace, as if the air had swallowed somebody

explanation.surface: The Derbyshire hills have a quality that makes people go missing up there.
explanation.walkthrough: High Peak is the Derbyshire district at the top of the Peak District, and the capital letters make it a place name; climb it and the air really does thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Climb high enough and the air thins, which is a feature of any high peak, while the idiom has people vanish into thin air.

clue.text: In other words, what to do with broken-down car

parts.words: what to do with broken-down car
parts.note: a car that will not go has to be pulled away behind another vehicle
the car is the thing being pulled, referred to as it

explanation.surface: Your car has broken down and somebody is telling you what happens next.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words of the wordplay and the two of the answer are not the same two — the break moves one letter along, and that is the whole joke. TO WIT is the lawyer's 'namely'.
explanation.definitionFit: To wit introduces a restatement — namely, that is to say — which is the job 'in other words' announces in ordinary English.

clue.text: Imogen's model daughter required to be paid

parts.note: Imogen is the setter, so her own name taken as her voice is I'm
to model for a painter or a camera is to pose
d is the family-tree abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: The setter's daughter does modelling work and is waiting to be paid for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Imogen is the setter's own pseudonym, so 'Imogen's' is her saying I'm — the setter writing herself into her clue, which is a habit worth expecting on a Saturday.
explanation.definitionFit: A tax, a fine or a levy that is imposed is one you are required to pay: the levying sense of the word, not the intruding one.

clue.text: Writer covering India with nothing about treatment for infection

indicators.note: the writing tool wraps around the India letter

parts.note: a pencil is a writing tool
India is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for I

indicators.note: turned about, the nothing word is read backwards

parts.note: nil means nothing

explanation.surface: A writer covering India returns empty-handed and needs treatment for a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' is a pencil, not an author; it covers I, and NIL turned 'about' gives LIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Penicillin was the first widely used antibiotic, a treatment for bacterial infection.

clue.text: Mostly ease off work, getting handouts

indicators.note: Most of a phrase is all of it bar the end, so the last letter of what follows never gets written down.

parts.note: easing off at work is doing less of it, and the two words run together

explanation.surface: Somebody who mostly slacks at work and lives off what other people give them.
explanation.walkthrough: The dole is the British word for unemployment benefit, and to dole something out is to hand it round in portions — the same word doing both jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Doles are amounts handed out in portions, the dole being Britain's unemployment payment, so 'handouts' matches sense and plural exactly.

clue.text: Dance music from Disney on air

indicators.note: Something on air is heard rather than read, so what counts is how the words sound, not how they are spelt.

parts.note: Disney's first name was Walt, so music that belongs to him is Walt's — and that possessive is what you say aloud

explanation.surface: Music from the Disney studio being played on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On air' is broadcasting in the surface and sounding in the wordplay. Said aloud, the possessive S hardens into a Z, and that hardening is the whole mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: A waltz is the ballroom dance in three-four time, so 'Dance' names the answer by its plainest category.

clue.text: More wary than anyone of lake, most unearthly

parts.note: L is the map-maker's short form for lake
unearthly is eerie, and 'most' asks for the superlative of it

explanation.surface: Nobody is more nervous than this of a lake that looks thoroughly haunted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More wary than anyone' is a superlative spelled out the long way, which is the tip-off that the answer ends -EST. Leery is the wary one, as in leery of a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: To be leery of something is to be wary of it, so the person warier than anybody else is the leeriest of them.

clue.text: Whippet?

parts.note: read as one word it is a breed of racing dog, which is all the surface offers; split it after the fourth letter and it asks for two things at once, a whip and a pet

explanation.surface: A whippet, the slender racing dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the only signal you get. Break the word in two and both halves define the answer: a cat-o'-nine-tails is a whip, and a cat is a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat is the commonest household pet, and the cat-o'-nine-tails was the navy's whip, so one split word covers both senses.

clue.text: Calvin's business giving off bad smell gets halved

parts.note: CO is short for company, a business
olid is a rare word meaning foul-smelling

indicators.note: the word is cut in half, keeping only its first two letters

explanation.surface: Calvin's company is halved after it starts to stink.
explanation.walkthrough: Calvin Coolidge was the 30th US president. OLID, meaning fetid, is uncommon, and 'halved' leaves GE from GETS.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin Coolidge was President of the United States from 1923 to 1929, so the surname is the famous Calvin.

clue.text: Changing hands, more recent post

indicators.note: right and left are the two hands, so the right letter is changed to the left letter

parts.note: newer means more recent

explanation.surface: A newer job has gone to someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing hands' sounds like a sale; here R, for right, becomes L, for left. 'post' is a staircase post, not a job.
explanation.definitionFit: A newel is the central post of a spiral staircase or the post at the end of a banister.

clue.text: Boot her out? There are strings attached to that

definitions.text: There are strings attached to that
definitions.note: The setter describes the answer rather than naming it: a whole sentence stands where a noun would normally go, and it tells you what the thing has rather than what it is.

indicators.note: Boot somebody out and they finish up anywhere but where they were, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: seven letters of raw material, the two words run together

explanation.surface: Evicting her comes with conditions — there are strings attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strings attached' is the idiom for conditions in the surface and a literal statement in the answer, which is a bass lute the size of a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorbo is a long-necked bass lute, so a sentence about strings hanging off something is a fair description of it.

clue.text: Regularly take free measures of wood cut as logs

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals, here the second and fourth

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of free
a cord is a measure of cut firewood, 128 cubic feet

explanation.surface: Collect cut firewood for nothing to burn as logs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly take' picks alternate letters of FREE, giving RE. A cord is a stacked measure of cut timber. 'logs' is the verb sense here: records.
explanation.definitionFit: Logs, as a noun, are written records of events, such as a ship's log.

clue.text: Chorister sang out, missing note in the story of Cinderella

indicators.note: sung out of order, the letters are rearranged
the note letter is missing, taken from the pool of letters

explanation.surface: A choirboy sang badly, missing a note in a pantomime.
explanation.walkthrough: CHORISTER SANG has thirteen letters; 'missing note' takes away N, and 'out' rearranges the other twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinderella rises from servant to princess, the classic tale of going from poverty to wealth.

clue.text: See 22
Huge energy in description of 60s London

indicators.note: 'In' drops the letter just named inside the word that follows, between one half of it and the other.

parts.note: the city of the 1960s was called swinging, after its music and fashion boom
E is energy in physics, as in Einstein's equation

explanation.surface: London in the sixties, described by its enormous energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Swinging London was Carnaby Street and the King's Road, the tag the magazines gave the city. One extra E separates that word from the one meaning severe.
explanation.definitionFit: Swingeing means severe or very large — a swingeing tax rise is a huge one — and it is a different word from swinging.

clue.text: Stitched up by all the cardinals

parts.note: the cardinal points are the four compass directions, and south leads off here
east is the second of the four, in the order this entry needs
west is third, the one facing the direction that started it
north closes the set of four

explanation.surface: The cardinals have stitched somebody up between them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinals' wants to be the men in red hats and means the cardinal points instead — north, south, east and west, all four of them turning up in a fresh order.
explanation.definitionFit: Sewn is the past participle of sew, so anything stitched is sewn; the idiom's other sense, being framed, belongs to the surface.

clue.text: Artist's ascetic discipline: cycling backwards

indicators.note: the result is then read in reverse
the letters cycle round, the last one moving to the front

parts.note: yoga is a Hindu discipline of self-control

explanation.surface: An artist's strict spiritual practice is reversed on a bike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves YOGA's final A to the front to make AYOG, and 'backwards' reverses that. Goya was the Spanish painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Francisco Goya was a celebrated Spanish painter and printmaker.

clue.text: A number in the vicinity

definitions.meaning: not the counting kind but a thing that numbs, which the dentist injects
the ordinary adjective for whatever is close at hand

explanation.surface: A figure somewhere close by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is not the counting one but a thing that numbs. Say it numb-er, with the B sounded, and the anaesthetic the dentist gives you is what the clue is asking for.
explanation.definitionFit: A local is the anaesthetic that numbs one part of you, and local also means nearby — the pub sense comes from that same closeness.

clue.text: Come close, perhaps threatening weaver

definitions.note: A weaver is normally the person at the machine rather than the machine itself, so the setter is using the agent noun for the thing that does the weaving.
definitions.meaning: the verb for something large drawing near, a headland or a deadline
the frame that holds the warp threads while the weft goes across

explanation.surface: Something drawing near in a way that feels like a threat.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma is the seam: everything before it is a verb and the single word after it is a machine, which is why the clue reads as one continuous menace.
explanation.definitionFit: To loom is to come into view large and close, often menacingly; a loom is also the frame cloth is woven on.

clue.text: Flimsy Caribbean agent

parts.note: the West Indies are the Caribbean islands, WI on a cricket scoreboard
an agent working undercover is a spy

explanation.surface: A frail-looking secret agent from the islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caribbean' is the West Indies, shortened the way cricket shortens it. The definition is the single word at the front, which reads as part of the picture and is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wispy is thin and insubstantial, a wisp of hair or smoke, which is what calling a thing flimsy says about it.

clue.text: See to twig confused for a different twig

indicators.note: Something confused is in disarray, and letters in disarray have lost the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: nine letters of raw material, the three words run together

explanation.surface: One twig gets mistaken for another twig entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twig' appears twice and means something different each time: the first is raw material, the second is the definition, British slang for catching on.
explanation.definitionFit: To twig something is British slang for suddenly understanding it, which is exactly what getting wise to a thing means.
